reckoner.distinguishingFeature: A balanced default with an explicit Explain phase after inquiry.
reckoner.bestScienceFit: Most Stage 4–5 focus areas; the strongest default for early career teachers.
reckoner.commonPitfall: Relabelling existing lessons with E headings without changing their order.
reckoner.evidenceSummary: A 2023 meta-analysis of 61 randomised trials found large gains in science achievement for 3E/5E/7E models (g = 0.87).

introduction.lead: The 5E model gives you a research-informed sequence that starts from what students already think and moves them towards scientific understanding.
introduction.purposeStatement:
This guide helps undergraduate and early career teachers design, check and refine 5E sequences
for the NSW Science 7–10 Syllabus (2023). It explains the essential features of each phase,
shows what each phase looks like done well and done badly, and gives you a checklist for
auditing a program before you teach it.
introduction.audience: Pre-service teachers in secondary science method units, and teachers in their first years.
introduction.howToUse:
Read the theory and model overview once. Keep the phase cards, misapplications and checklist
open while you plan. Try each worked sequence's prediction question before reading why it works.

theory.summary:
Students build new understanding by testing it against ideas they already hold. The 5E model
makes that process visible and productive, and times explanation so it lands on prepared ground.

foundations.idea: Learning is triggered when experience does not fit existing mental models, leading to assimilation or accommodation.
foundations.designImplication: Engage and Explore are built to create a productive mismatch before any explanation.

foundations.idea: Students abandon a prior conception only when dissatisfied with it, and the new idea is intelligible, plausible and fruitful.
foundations.designImplication: Engage and Explore create dissatisfaction; Explain makes the idea intelligible and plausible; Elaborate shows it is fruitful.

foundations.idea: Understanding is built through talk, shared representations and guided support within the zone of proximal development.
foundations.designImplication: Group exploration, argument from evidence and teacher scaffolding in Explain are social processes, planned as such.

critiques.claim: Minimally guided instruction is less effective than explicit instruction for novices.
critiques.response: The 5E model does not withhold explanation. It places explicit teaching in Explain, after students have experience to attach it to.

roles.teacher: Facilitates Engage and Explore, teaches explicitly in Explain, designs transfer in Elaborate, and assesses throughout.
roles.learner: Predicts, investigates, explains with evidence, applies ideas in new contexts, and reflects on how their thinking changed.

sequence.summary: Five phases forming one conceptual storyline, with formative assessment running through every phase.
sequence.diagramMermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Engage] --> B[Explore] --> C[Explain] --> D[Elaborate] --> E[Evaluate]
  E -. next sequence .-> A
sequence.scaleNote: A 5E sequence is usually 4–12 lessons around one big question, not one lesson with five segments.

phases.name: Engage
phases.job: Create a need to know and make students' current thinking visible.
essentialFeatures: A concrete phenomenon, discrepant event or problem linked to the big idea
Students commit to a prediction or explanation before any teaching
The teacher records student ideas to revisit later
Short, usually one lesson or less
learnerMoves: States and commits to a current explanation

lookFors.question: Is the hook conceptually linked to the big idea, or just entertaining?
lookFors.strongEvidence: The phenomenon is the one the sequence will explain.
lookFors.weakEvidence: An unrelated video or demonstration used for attention only.

lookFors.question: Are student ideas elicited and recorded?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Predictions are written down and kept for later comparison.

lookFors.question: Does Engage raise the question the sequence will answer?
lookFors.strongEvidence: A driving question is posed and displayed.
lookFors.weakEvidence: The lesson moves straight to definitions.

examples.title: Where did the salt go?
examples.body:
Students weigh water and salt separately, predict the mass once the salt dissolves, and write why.
Many predict a loss because the salt "disappears". The teacher photographs the prediction chart
and asks how the class could find out where the salt went.
examples.diagnosis: Linked phenomenon, committed predictions and a driving question for the whole sequence.

examples.title: A spectacular but unrelated video
examples.body: A video of an exothermic reaction, then "Copy the definitions of solute and solvent."
examples.diagnosis: A hook, but not an Engage. The video is unrelated to dissolving and no thinking is surfaced.

phases.name: Explore
phases.job: Give every student a shared, concrete experience of the phenomenon before the scientific explanation.
essentialFeatures: Hands-on or minds-on investigation in which students generate evidence
Teacher questions and probes but does not supply the answer
Students record observations, test predictions and notice patterns
Structure calibrated on the structured, guided or open continuum
formativeChecks: Checks of data tables and variable control

lookFors.question: Does the investigation come before the formal explanation?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students would still need to think even if they knew the answer.
lookFors.weakEvidence: A confirmation practical run after the theory.

lookFors.question: Is the data the students' own?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students generate and record their own evidence.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Results are given or a conclusion is pre-scaffolded.

lookFors.question: Does the activity produce the evidence Explain will draw on?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Explain explicitly uses the Explore results.

examples.title: Antacid tablets at four temperatures
examples.body:
Groups time effervescent tablets in water at four temperatures, then crushed versus whole.
The teacher asks what students notice and what might be happening to the particles,
without introducing collision theory yet.
examples.diagnosis: Students generate evidence before explanation, and the data sets up Explain.

examples.title: Proving what was already taught
examples.body: Collision theory is taught first, then students follow a recipe with a fill-in-the-blank conclusion.
examples.diagnosis: A confirmation practical in the Explore slot. Students verify rather than investigate.

phases.name: Explain
phases.job: Help students make sense of the Explore experience by building the scientific explanation from it.
essentialFeatures: Students explain first, in their own words, using their evidence
Teacher introduces concepts, terms and models linked to what students observed
Direct instruction belongs here
Students compare their Engage ideas with the scientific explanation

lookFors.question: Do students explain first, before the teacher?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Groups present and interpret their own data.
lookFors.weakEvidence: The teacher explains and students copy notes.

lookFors.question: Does the explanation refer back to the class's own data?
lookFors.strongEvidence: The teacher cites group results when introducing concepts.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Explanation is disconnected from the investigation.

lookFors.question: Are multiple representations used?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Macroscopic, particulate, symbolic and graphical views are connected.

lookFors.question: Are the Engage ideas explicitly revisited?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students name what has changed in their thinking.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Prior ideas are never returned to.

examples.title: Newton's second law from the class's trolley data
examples.body:
Groups present their trolley graphs. The teacher introduces F = ma using the class data,
draws force diagrams on the groups' own set-ups, and addresses the idea that a moving object
needs a force to keep moving.
examples.diagnosis: Students explain first, and the formal idea is built from their data and prior ideas.

examples.title: Three lessons of slides
examples.body: Three consecutive lessons of slides and notes on Newton's laws, two weeks after the practical.
examples.diagnosis: Explanation is present, but constructivist sequencing is lost.

phases.name: Elaborate
phases.job: Deepen and transfer understanding by applying it to a new situation.
essentialFeatures: A new context, problem or application that requires the concept
Opportunities to extend to more complex systems or socio-scientific issues
A natural home for design tasks and depth study work
Students use scientific language and argue from evidence
teacherMoves: Poses a new problem or context

lookFors.question: Is the context genuinely different from Explore?
lookFors.strongEvidence: A new setting that requires transfer.
lookFors.weakEvidence: A repeat of the Explore activity or textbook questions.

lookFors.question: Does the task demand the concept?
lookFors.strongEvidence: The task cannot be completed without using the concept.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Students can succeed without the science.

lookFors.question: Is cognitive demand higher than in Explore?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Students apply, analyse, design or evaluate.

examples.title: Drinkable water for a remote community
examples.body:
Students design a low-cost system to produce drinkable water from muddy, salty water, justify each
separation step by the property it exploits, test a prototype and evaluate its limits.
examples.diagnosis: A new context that demands the concept, with higher cognitive demand.

examples.title: Textbook questions 1–15
examples.body: Questions that repeat the definitions from Explain.
examples.diagnosis: No new context, no transfer and no increase in demand.

phases.name: Evaluate
phases.job: Give students and teacher evidence of learning, and let students see their own conceptual change.
essentialFeatures: Formative assessment runs through every phase
The final task is aligned with learning intentions and success criteria
Students revisit their Engage ideas and explain how their thinking changed
Content and Working scientifically outcomes are both assessed
formativeChecks: Summative task marked against success criteria

lookFors.question: Is the assessment aligned with the outcomes actually taught?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Tasks map to the stated outcomes and success criteria.
lookFors.weakEvidence: Assessment covers content not taught, or omits Working scientifically.

lookFors.question: Does it test understanding and application, not just recall?
Do students return to their initial ideas?
lookFors.strongEvidence: I used to think… now I think… because…

lookFors.question: Are formative checks built into every phase?
lookFors.strongEvidence: Checks appear throughout and inform adjustment.

examples.title: Where does a tree's mass come from?
examples.body:
Students annotate their Engage drawings with evidence from the sequence, then explain an
unfamiliar plant's growth using photosynthesis and gas exchange.
examples.diagnosis: Aligned, application-focused, and makes conceptual change visible.

examples.title: A recall test in week 8
examples.body: A 30-question recall test at the end, with no formative checks during the sequence.
examples.diagnosis: The teacher discovers too late that most students still believe plants eat soil.

workedSequences.title: Why do things slow down and stop?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: Why do things slow down and stop?
learningIntentions: Friction is a contact force that opposes motion
Unbalanced forces change an object's motion
How to design a fair test and represent data
targetConceptions: A moving object stops because it runs out of force

steps.activity: Slide a puck across carpet, lino and ice. Students predict why it stops and whether it would stop on perfect ice.
steps.formativeCheck: Individual prediction cards

steps.activity: Pull a weighted shoe across surfaces with a spring balance; vary one factor and record force.
steps.formativeCheck: Questioning; check tables and variable control

steps.activity: PhET Forces and Motion simulation with friction removed; students revise predictions.
steps.formativeCheck: Revised prediction on the thinking wall

steps.activity: Groups present patterns; teacher introduces friction, balanced and unbalanced forces, and force arrows from class data.
steps.formativeCheck: Mini-whiteboard force diagrams

scaffoldSlots.prompt: Which group results would you use to introduce friction, and in what order?

steps.activity: Worked examples and guided practice drawing force diagrams for everyday situations.
steps.formativeCheck: Exit ticket with one diagram and explanation

steps.activity: Design challenge to improve grip for a ramp, a shoe for wet tiles, or a carnival sled; justify with forces.
steps.formativeCheck: Design log checkpoints; peer feedback

scaffoldSlots.prompt: What evidence would show a student is using friction to justify a design choice, not just trial and error?

steps.activity: Students revisit their lesson 1 card and explain a curling stone or air-hockey puck with force diagrams.
steps.formativeCheck: Summative task against success criteria

whyItWorks: The Engage question is the one Evaluate answers, so the storyline closes
Explore generates the data Explain uses
The simulation removes friction in a way no school lab can
Elaborate shifts to design, raising cognitive demand
Formative checks in every phase allow adjustment
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, which feature of this sequence do you think does most to shift the target conception, and why?

workedSequences.title: What makes something alive, and how do we sort living things?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: What makes something alive, and how do we sort living things?
learningIntentions: All living things are made of cells
Plant, animal and microbial cells share some structures and differ in others
Scientists classify organisms using observable structural features
targetConceptions: Plants and fungi are not made of cells
Cells are flat, like textbook diagrams
Living things are things that move
Classification groups are fixed and obvious

steps.activity:
Card sort of a candle flame, a seed, yeast granules, a lichen-covered rock, a crystal, a mushroom
and a virus image into "alive" and "not alive". Each group writes the rule it used; rules go on a
class thinking wall.
steps.formativeCheck: Photograph of each group's sort and rule

steps.activity:
Microscopy rotation: onion epidermis, cheek cells (or prepared slides), Elodea leaf, yeast in sugar
water and pond water. Students draw at two magnifications, estimate size, and list what all samples
have in common.
steps.formativeCheck: Check drawings for scale, labels and magnification; questioning at each station

scaffoldSlots.prompt: What question would you ask at the Elodea station to find out whether a student thinks plants are made of cells?

steps.activity:
Groups share drawings. The teacher introduces cell theory, key organelles (nucleus, cell membrane,
cell wall, chloroplast, vacuole) and unicellular versus multicellular organisms, using students' own
images and a 3D cell model to challenge the flat-cell idea.
steps.formativeCheck: Mini-whiteboard Venn diagram of plant and animal cells

steps.activity:
The teacher models building a dichotomous key for classroom objects, then for living things, and
introduces kingdoms and binomial names.
steps.formativeCheck: Exit ticket using a short key to identify two organisms

scaffoldSlots.prompt: Which students' drawings from lessons 2–4 would you use to show a feature that separates plants from fungi, and why?

steps.activity:
Students build a dichotomous key for 8–10 local organisms from a schoolyard survey or specimen photos,
then test it on a peer. Extension: compare Western taxonomy with an Aboriginal classification system
for local plants and animals, developed with local community input, and discuss what each is
designed to do.
steps.formativeCheck: Peer test of keys; teacher feedback on the features chosen

steps.activity:
Students revise their lesson 1 sort with evidence and complete "I used to think… now I think…
because…". Short task: classify an unfamiliar organism from images and justify using cell and
structural evidence.
steps.formativeCheck: Summative task against success criteria

whyItWorks: The Engage sort surfaces fuzzy criteria for life that students test and refine throughout
Students see real cells before a labelled diagram, so vocabulary attaches to their own observations
Elaborate moves from recognising structures to using them to classify, raising cognitive demand
Comparing knowledge systems shows classification as a human, purposeful activity
workedSequences.watchFor:
The temptation to open with a labelled animal cell diagram. For biology-trained teachers this feels
efficient, but it turns lessons 2–4 into a spot-the-organelle exercise rather than an investigation.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, why might this sequence delay the labelled cell diagram until lesson 5? What would be lost if it came first?

workedSequences.title: How does a disease spread through a community, and what is the best way to stop it?
workedSequences.bigQuestion: How does a disease spread through a community, and what is the best way to stop it?
learningIntentions: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens transmitted in specific ways
The immune system responds to pathogens
Vaccination, hygiene and public health measures reduce spread, and data can be used to evaluate them
targetConceptions: Vaccines only protect the person vaccinated

steps.activity:
A hypothetical scenario: half a Year 9 class is absent with the same illness after camp. Students
answer individually: what caused it, how did it spread, and what should the school do? Answers are
recorded, then pooled.
steps.formativeCheck: Written initial explanations collected

steps.activity:
Simulated outbreak: each student has a cup of clear liquid, one secretly "infected" with dilute sodium
carbonate. Students exchange liquid over three rounds, test with indicator, and use exchange records
to trace patient zero. Repeat with a "vaccinated" subgroup whose cups cannot be infected.
steps.formativeCheck: Transmission tables and tracing logic checked

steps.activity:
Groups analyse a real data set, such as measles cases against vaccination coverage or notifiable
disease data, describe patterns, and write a hypothesis explaining them.
steps.formativeCheck: Hypothesis statements reviewed

scaffoldSlots.prompt: What would a weak hypothesis look like here, and what feedback would move it towards a testable one?

steps.activity:
Groups present findings. The teacher introduces pathogen types (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists,
parasites), modes of transmission, the immune response and herd immunity, linking repeatedly to the
simulation and data, and explicitly addresses the idea that antibiotics cure viruses.
steps.formativeCheck: Mini-whiteboards matching pathogen, transmission and control measure

steps.activity:
Case study of John Snow's cholera map and the rise of germ theory. Students annotate their Engage
answers with new concepts.
steps.formativeCheck: Annotated Engage response

steps.activity:
Students choose a disease relevant to a community (a vaccine-preventable disease, a zoonotic disease,
or trachoma in remote communities) and produce an evidence-based public health recommendation. They
evaluate one online claim about the disease for legitimacy and weigh ethical considerations. Where
relevant, include Aboriginal community-controlled health perspectives, developed with community.
steps.formativeCheck: Draft recommendation conference; claim-evaluation checkpoint

scaffoldSlots.prompt: Which criteria would you give students for judging whether an online health claim is legitimate?

steps.activity:
Students revisit the camp scenario and rewrite their response with scientific reasoning. Short task:
explain a new outbreak scenario, identify the pathogen type and propose justified control measures.
steps.formativeCheck: Summative task against success criteria

whyItWorks: The simulation lets students experience exponential spread and herd immunity before they hear the terms
Real data moves Explore beyond the lab and builds towards Stage 5 data outcomes
Elaborate is a genuine transfer task with ethical and evidence-evaluation dimensions
The Engage scenario returns in Evaluate, so students can see how far their reasoning has moved
workedSequences.watchFor:
Letting Elaborate become a poster about a disease. The recommendation must use transmission and immunity
concepts, and the claim evaluation must cite evidence.
workedSequences.safetyNotes:
Follow your school's chemical safety procedures for the simulation, and your sector's microbiology
guidelines if you add culturing (sealed plates, no opening, correct disposal). Disease topics can touch
students' experience of illness or loss: keep the Engage scenario hypothetical and give students choice
of disease in Elaborate.
workedSequences.predictPrompt: Before reading on, what does the simulation in lessons 2–3 let students experience that a lecture on herd immunity could not?

misapplications.name: Labels without logic
misapplications.looksLike: Existing lessons re-badged with E headings; order unchanged.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Explanation still precedes experience, so there is no mechanism for conceptual change.
misapplications.fix: Rebuild around one big question and move practical work before explanation.

misapplications.name: Five Es in one lesson
misapplications.looksLike: Ten minutes per phase, every lesson.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: No time to explore or transfer; phases become rituals.

misapplications.name: Engage as entertainment
misapplications.looksLike: A fun video or demonstration with no link to the concept.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Motivation without elicitation; prior ideas stay hidden.
misapplications.fix: Require a prediction or explanation and record it.

misapplications.name: Explore as confirmation
misapplications.looksLike: A recipe practical run after the theory.
misapplications.fix: Run the investigation first and hold back the answer.

misapplications.name: Explain as teacher monologue
misapplications.looksLike: Lessons of slides and notes with no student talk.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Students' ideas are bypassed and misconceptions persist.
misapplications.fix: Students explain first; build on their data.

misapplications.name: Explore without Explain
misapplications.whyItUndermines: Students leave with vague or wrong ideas.
misapplications.fix: Always follow Explore with explicit sense-making.

misapplications.name: Missing Elaborate
misapplications.looksLike: The sequence ends at Explain, then a test.
misapplications.whyItUndermines: No transfer; understanding stays bound to one context.
misapplications.fix: Plan a new context that demands the concept.

misapplications.name: Evaluate only at the end
misapplications.whyItUndermines: No chance to respond to misconceptions during the sequence.
misapplications.fix: Embed formative checks in every phase.

items.text: One big question anchors the sequence and Evaluate returns to it
Content and Working scientifically outcomes are named and taught
Target alternative conceptions are identified in advance
The hook is linked to the big idea
Student predictions are recorded for later
Students explain first using Explore evidence
Formative checks appear in every phase
Students reflect on how their thinking changed
Adjustments are planned for EAL/D learners, students with disability and high potential students
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives are authentic and developed with community
Practical work has a risk assessment

syllabusAlignment.depthStudies: A depth study fits an extended Elaborate phase, or can be designed as its own 5E cycle with a student-generated question.
syllabusAlignment.dataScience: Real data sets can serve as the Explore experience before modelling or claim evaluation is introduced.

inclusion.eald: Explore gives shared concrete experience before technical language; pre-teach vocabulary in Explain with visuals and sentence frames.
inclusion.disability: Plan adjustments to practical tasks, recording formats and communication modes; Life Skills outcomes may apply.
inclusion.highPotential: Open up Explore with student-designed variables and deepen Elaborate with complex systems.
inclusion.aboriginalPerspectives: Engage and Elaborate suit authentic, place-based connections developed with local Aboriginal community.

nesting.how: Use a Predict–Observe–Explain to surface and challenge the target conception.
Use a Science Writing Heuristic template to structure claims and evidence.
Run an Argument-Driven Inquiry across Explore and Explain when the sequence targets argument from evidence.
Add a socio-scientific deliberation as the transfer task.
Set the inquiry level to learner readiness.

reflectionPrompts.prompt: Think of a science idea you misunderstood at school. What would an Engage and Explore sequence have needed to do to change your mind?
coachFollowUps: What evidence would have convinced you?
Why might direct explanation alone not have worked?

reflectionPrompts.prompt: Where does the 5E model sit in relation to the critique of minimally guided instruction, and what design choices keep it on the right side?
coachFollowUps: Which phase carries the explicit guidance?
What happens if Explain is skipped?

reflectionPrompts.prompt: Choose a Stage 4 or Stage 5 focus area, identify one alternative conception, and design an Engage activity that surfaces it.
coachFollowUps: How will you record students' ideas?
When in the sequence will you return to them?

never: Never return a rewritten or completed teaching program in tutor mode
Never fill scaffold slots on the learner's behalf
Never cite an outcome code that is not in the syllabus whitelist
Never answer a reflection prompt; ask follow-up questions only
